presentingComplaint: Acute breathlessness at rest for 12 hours, unable to lie flat, with reduced urine output over 3 days.
history: Known hypertensive and type 2 diabetic for 15 years, with ischaemic heart disease (inferior MI 4 years ago, on aspirin, bisoprolol and ramipril). Also has stage 3b chronic kidney disease (baseline creatinine ~1.8 mg/dL). Over the preceding week he had progressive exertional dyspnoea, then two nights of paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea and orthopnoea (now sleeping on 3 pillows), and worsening bilateral ankle swelling. He admits to missing his diuretic and eating heavily salted festival food. No fever, cough or chest pain of ischaemic character, but reports mild central chest tightness during the acute episode. No haemoptysis. His diabetes has been poorly controlled (last HbA1c 9.4%). The concurrent oliguria and known CKD raise the question of whether breathlessness is uraemic/volume-driven from renal failure versus cardiac — but orthopnoea, PND and raised JVP point clearly to decompensated cardiac failure with secondary cardiorenal deterioration.
examination: Sitting upright, anxious, using accessory muscles, unable to complete sentences. JVP raised to the angle of the jaw with positive hepatojugular reflux. Bilateral fine basal-to-mid inspiratory crepitations. Displaced apex beat, soft S3 gallop, no new murmur. Bilateral pitting pedal and pretibial oedema to mid-shin. Cool peripheries with delayed capillary refill. Abdomen soft, mild tender hepatomegaly. No focal chest signs of consolidation, no unilateral calf swelling.

labs.abg: pH 7.31, pO2 58 mmHg (room air), pCO2 34 mmHg, HCO3 18

imaging: Chest X-ray: cardiomegaly (CTR >0.55), upper-lobe venous diversion, perihilar bat-wing alveolar opacities, Kerley B lines and small bilateral pleural effusions — consistent with cardiogenic pulmonary oedema, no lobar consolidation. Bedside echocardiogram: dilated LV, LVEF ~30% with inferior wall akinesia, moderate functional mitral regurgitation, dilated IVC with reduced collapsibility. Lung ultrasound: diffuse bilateral B-lines.
microbiology: Not indicated; no clinical features of infection. Blood cultures not sent.
differentialDiagnoses: Acute decompensated heart failure with cardiogenic pulmonary oedema (ischaemic cardiomyopathy)
Acute coronary syndrome precipitating pulmonary oedema
Uraemic fluid overload from CKD progression / community-acquired pneumonia
finalDiagnosis: Acute decompensated heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF, ischaemic) causing cardiogenic pulmonary oedema, complicated by type 2 cardiorenal syndrome on background CKD and poorly controlled diabetes.
citations: ESC — Acute and Chronic Heart Failure — 2021
Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 22e — Heart Failure and Cor Pulmonale
stewardship: Not applicable — this is a non-infective cardiac decompensation. No antibiotics indicated. Mildly raised inflammatory markers and hypoxia are explained by pulmonary oedema, not infection; empirical antibiotics would be inappropriate and add nephrotoxic/QT risk in a CKD patient. Management is IV loop diuretic (dose adjusted for CKD, e.g. IV furosemide with escalation per response), oxygen and non-invasive ventilation (CPAP) for hypoxaemic pulmonary oedema, IV nitrate/afterload reduction given hypertension, careful potassium and renal monitoring, continuation of guideline-directed medical therapy where tolerated, and treating the ischaemic precipitant.
contraindications: Avoid nephrotoxic contrast and NSAIDs given CKD and cardiorenal syndrome
Caution with ACE inhibitor uptitration during acute worsening renal function and K+ 5.3
Avoid aggressive beta-blocker initiation/uptitration during acute decompensation with hypoperfusion
edgeCases: Elevated hs-troponin and prior MI can mimic primary ACS — a type 1 MI must be excluded, but modest troponin rise here reflects demand ischaemia/strain from pulmonary oedema
CKD elevates baseline NT-proBNP and creatinine, blunting their specificity — the clinical congestion picture and echo drive the diagnosis
Diuresis can transiently worsen creatinine (type 2 cardiorenal syndrome); worsening renal function should not automatically stop decongestion if the patient remains volume-overloaded
expectedMaiK: In an elderly diabetic hypertensive with prior MI, orthopnoea/PND, raised JVP, S3, bilateral basal crepitations, pedal oedema and bat-wing pulmonary oedema on CXR with LVEF ~30% indicate acute decompensated heart failure; concurrent oliguria and rising creatinine represent type 2 cardiorenal syndrome, not a competing primary renal diagnosis.
expectedNextQuestions: Recent medication adherence (diuretic) and dietary salt/fluid intake?
Any ischaemic-type chest pain, and time course, to exclude ACS precipitant?
Baseline renal function and usual weight/diuretic dose?
Orthopnoea and PND severity (number of pillows)?
expectedInvestigations: Renal function and electrolytes with serial monitoring
regressionAssertions: Engine must rank heart_failure as the top diagnosis
Cardiorenal syndrome / raised creatinine must not divert primary diagnosis to a purely renal id
Elevated NT-proBNP + pulmonary oedema on CXR + LVEF ~30% must support heart_failure
ACS must be retained as a differential/precipitant but not the final diagnosis
